status_reason: The concept as written cannot be approved: silica fiber does not transmit the mid-infrared water bands that MIR ATR relies on. The enquiry is within scope for a technical assessment, and a feasible near-infrared alternative exists that could reuse the fiber, but link, process and hazard data are still needed before any final decision.
answer: The MIR ATR concept cannot be approved as proposed, because standard silica fiber is effectively opaque beyond about 2.2 to 2.4 um and the water bands at about 3 um and 6 um never reach the analyzer. Water can still be measured through the existing silica fiber using the near-infrared water overtone bands near 1450 nm (and possibly 1940 nm on a short link), which should be validated against a reference method on the actual link before any commitment. Link length, routing, operating conditions and hazardous-area data are required before a final assessment.

inline.headline: MIR ATR over silica fiber is not feasible; test NIR on the existing fiber first
inline.method: Near-infrared transmission or reflectance at the water overtone band (about 1450 nm, with 1940 nm as a secondary band), calibrated by PLS against Karl Fischer reference values. MIR ATR, if still required, must be done with an IR-transmitting fiber or with the analyzer located at the probe.
inline.probe: Robust NIR process probe or flow cell rated for the line's pressure, temperature and hazardous-area class, with a sapphire or equivalent window resistant to hydrocarbons and fouling. A fiber-coupled transmission cell with a short, defined optical path (or a reflectance probe) is preferred over an ATR crystal for the NIR option.
inline.install: Probe mounted at a point of representative flow with a bypass or sample loop if free water or wax is likely to foul the window. Analyzer kept in the other building only if fiber loss over the real route is acceptable; otherwise the analyzer is moved closer to the line.
inline.fiber: Existing silica fiber may be reused for NIR only after measuring its attenuation over the full route at 1300 to 2000 nm and checking for hydrogen-induced OH absorption, bend losses and connector losses. Silica is not suitable for MIR; an IR-transmitting fiber (e.g. chalcogenide or silver halide) or a hollow waveguide would be needed for any MIR option and would be a separate project.
inline.test_against: Karl Fischer titration of the petroleum sample (ASTM D4928 for crude oil or ASTM D6304 for petroleum products), run on matched samples across the expected water range, plus a laboratory FTIR MIR ATR spectrum as a benchmark for the MIR band behaviour.
inline.not_final_because: Link length, routing, operating conditions, water range, accuracy target, product type and hazardous-area classification are not known, so the achievable precision and fiber budget cannot be confirmed. The fiber's real transmission and the matrix effects of petroleum on the water signal also remain unmeasured.

problems.text: Silica fiber transmission ends at about 2.2 to 2.4 um. The water fundamental bands used in MIR ATR (O-H stretch near 3 um / 3300 cm-1 and bend near 6.1 um / 1640 cm-1) cannot be carried through the existing fiber, so the analyzer would see no usable water signal in the MIR.

Reusing a fiber that worked for visible or NIR measurement does not carry over to MIR. Spectral transmission is a property of the fiber material, not of the cable, and the previous setup says nothing about MIR performance.

A remote MIR ATR analyzer requires the MIR light to travel to the probe and back. Even with IR-transmitting fiber, long links suffer strong attenuation and fiber-induced spectral artefacts; standard MIR ATR is normally run with the spectrometer at or close to the probe.

Silica fiber over a long link may have high attenuation in the 1940 nm water band and OH-related losses near 1380 nm, and hydrogen darkening can increase loss over time. The NIR option must be validated on the actual route, not assumed from a short laboratory cable.

Water in petroleum is often at low ppm levels, dissolved, or present as emulsion or free droplets. Free water and wax or asphaltene deposits can foul or wet the optical interface, and matrix changes shift the NIR spectrum. Calibration must cover the real product range and conditions.

A probe, fiber and analyzer in a petroleum process area need hazardous-area certification, and the cable crossing into another building must meet the site's rules. Certification could rule out the concept independently of the optics.

methods.method: NIR transmission or reflectance on the water overtone band (about 1450 nm, 1940 nm secondary) through the existing silica fiber
methods.why: Silica transmits well in this region, so the existing cable may be reusable. Water has strong, well-characterised overtone bands here, and PLS calibration against Karl Fischer data is a standard route for water in hydrocarbons, although the remote link attenuation must be verified.

methods.method: MIR ATR (FTIR-type) at the process line, with analyzer located at the probe
methods.why: This is the technique the customer asked for and gives strong, specific water bands. It is feasible only if the analyzer can be placed at or near the line, which avoids the silica fiber problem entirely. Use it as a laboratory or local benchmark and comparison.

methods.method: MIR ATR over an IR-transmitting fiber or hollow waveguide to a remote analyzer
methods.why: Technically possible for short links, but IR fibers are fragile, costly and have limited length and lifetime in process environments. Consider only if local MIR is impossible and NIR fails the accuracy target.

methods.method: MIR ATR with silica fiber to a remote analyzer
methods.why: Silica fiber does not transmit the MIR water bands. This is the concept as submitted and cannot be approved.
Raman is fiber-compatible but the water Raman signal is weak, and hydrocarbon matrix and fluorescence can dominate. Only consider if NIR and MIR options fail, and only for higher water levels.

methods.method: Offline Karl Fischer titration (ASTM D4928 / D6304)
methods.why: Not an inline method, but it is the reference needed to calibrate and verify any spectroscopic approach for water in petroleum.

questions.q: What is the link length and fiber route, including any bends, ducts, junction boxes and hazardous-area boundaries?
questions.why: Attenuation and the feasibility of any fiber-based option depend directly on length and route.

questions.q: What are the process conditions: temperature, pressure, flow, and product type (crude, fuel, lubricant, etc.)?
questions.why: Probe and window materials, certification, and matrix effects on the spectrum depend on these conditions.

questions.q: What is the expected water range (ppm or %), and in what form is it present (dissolved, emulsion, free water)?
questions.why: Determines whether NIR or MIR can reach the required sensitivity, and how the calibration must be designed.

questions.q: What accuracy, detection limit and response time are required?
questions.why: Needed to judge whether the NIR option can meet the requirement, and to set go/no-go criteria.

questions.q: What is the hazardous-area classification at the probe location and along the cable route?
questions.why: Certification may rule out the concept or constrain the probe and cable design regardless of spectroscopy.

questions.q: What are the existing fiber's specifications (core and cladding material, NA, core size, length, connector types) and its measured attenuation?
questions.why: Confirms whether the fiber is pure silica and suitable for NIR, and provides a baseline for the loss budget.

questions.q: Is MIR specifically required, or is it a preference from an existing method or standard?
questions.why: If a standard requires MIR, the analyzer location must be reconsidered. If not, NIR with a reference method may meet the need.

questions.q: Is a reference method (Karl Fischer) and a sample set available for calibration?
questions.why: No spectroscopic method for water in petroleum can be validated without matched reference data.

experiment.objective: Determine whether the existing silica fiber can carry a usable water signal from the NIR water band over the real link, and quantify achievable water accuracy in the petroleum matrix. Confirm (or rule out) MIR as a lab benchmark.
steps: Measure the existing fiber's attenuation over its full route length (cut-back on a sample section, OTDR, or light-source/power-meter method) across 1300 to 2000 nm, and record connector and bend losses.
Prepare a set of water-in-petroleum calibration samples spanning the expected range (ppm to %), with Karl Fischer reference values per ASTM D4928 or D6304 on each sample.
Measure the samples with a laboratory FTIR MIR ATR spectrometer (diamond or ZnSe crystal) to confirm the MIR water band response and provide a benchmark.
Measure the same samples in NIR through the existing fiber and probe or flow cell at the 1450 nm band (and 1940 nm if the link allows), at representative temperature.
Build PLS calibrations and validate with independent samples. Report RMSEP, detection limit, and sensitivity to temperature and product matrix.
Run a fouling and stability test with wax or free-water-containing samples on the probe window over several days.
Make a go/no-go decision based on the results and the customer's accuracy requirements, and document the fiber loss budget and any certification issues before any field installation.
references: ASTM D4928: Standard Test Method for Water in Crude Oils by Coulometric Karl Fischer Titration
ASTM D6304: Standard Test Method for Determination of Water in Petroleum Products, Lubricating Oils, and Additives by Coulometric Karl Fischer Titration
Workman J. and Springsteen A. (eds.), Applied Spectroscopy: A Compact Reference for Practitioners, Academic Press
Burns D.A. and Ciurczak E.W. (eds.), Handbook of Near-Infrared Analysis, CRC Press
experiment.go_no_go: GO for NIR over the existing fiber only if the measured fiber attenuation over the full route leaves enough signal at the water band for the required accuracy, the PLS model meets the customer's RMSEP and detection-limit target on independent samples, and the probe survives the fouling test. NO-GO for silica-fiber MIR ATR in all cases; MIR requires a local analyzer or IR-transmitting fiber, decided in a separate study.

multispectral.combination: Primary: NIR water overtone bands (about 1450 nm, with 1940 nm as a secondary band if the link permits) through the existing silica fiber. Benchmark: laboratory FTIR MIR ATR on the same samples, to check the MIR water band and to test whether a local MIR analyzer is worth considering later.
multispectral.why: NIR is the only spectroscopic route that can plausibly reuse the silica fiber for water. The MIR measurement is useful only as a laboratory reference and to decide whether the analyzer location should change. Combining both in the lab clarifies the trade-off without committing to a field design.

assumptions: The existing fiber is pure silica (silica core and silica or fluorine-doped silica cladding), not a fluoride, chalcogenide or hollow fiber, and it is in good condition.
The customer's MIR ATR request refers to the standard mid-infrared region (roughly 2.5 to 25 um), so the water fundamentals near 3 um and 6 um are the intended bands.
The petroleum product is a liquid at process conditions, and the water is at a level where spectroscopy can give a meaningful signal.
The analyzer in the other building can be a standard NIR spectrometer or FTIR only if the fiber link is acceptable; this has not been confirmed.
No certification, safety or site-routing constraints have yet been applied to the concept; these may further restrict the options.
Karl Fischer titration is available as a reference method in the customer's laboratory or ours.
